items.title: RFI
items.stakes: Kit answered the contractor's RFI in ten minutes. The contractor's RF scan says three channels are under a TV signal.
items.clock: Before the revised answer is due.
items.reward: Eight clean channels, a checked answer — and Kit still asking questions.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #59 · AVERY'S LENS  An answer is a design decision  Answering a question from site is designing — it deserves the same checks, the same numbers and a second pair of eyes.  Kit's ten-minute RFI answer would have put three wireless mics inside a TV transmitter's channel.

items.alt: RFI 31 on a sheet: the question about a new local transmitter at 546–552 MHz, and Kit's answer in red: ‘No change required’, answered in ten minutes, no calculation, no checker.
items.caption: No calculation. No checker.

items.prompt: I moved the three that were in the channel. Nearest gaps. That fixes it, right?

options.label: “Let's check what those moves did to every product first.”
options.reply: …545 is two times 543 minus 541. Oh no.

options.label: “You should have checked the first time.”
options.reply: I know. I'm trying to fix it.

options.label: “What did you check before you answered?”
options.reply: Honestly? Nothing. It was ten minutes before a meeting.

items.prompt: 10:00. The contractor's scan disagrees with Kit's answer. What do you do with RFI 31?
items.risk: Mics that die on opening night.
timeout: The contractor orders frequencies from a wrong answer.

hints.text: What does the scan actually show against the plan?

options.label: Stand by it — the RFI is closed
options.result: Opening night: three mics hiss through Act One.
options.consequence: A closed answer isn't a correct one.

options.label: Reopen it: read the scan, check every carrier against the occupied range, and recompute
options.result: V3, V4 and V5 are inside 546–552 MHz.

options.label: Tell the contractor to buy radios in another band
options.result: Ruth: “For eight channels? On what evidence?”

options.label: Tell Ruth it was Kit's answer

items.title: Inside the channel.
items.body: The regulator's database: a new local digital TV service, licensed in March, on air last month across 546–552 MHz. The plan was drawn in January. V3 at 547.0, V4 at 548.5 and V5 at 550.0 MHz are all under it — and a TV transmitter is thousands of times stronger than a bodypack.
items.label: Test: what happens to those three — and what should the answer have started with?

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Kit and Maya beside a board. Third-order products: two f one minus f two, and two f two minus f one. Five-forty-one and five-forty-three make five-thirty-nine and five-forty-five. Five-forty-five is where you moved V3. …I answered the RFI without doing that, didn't I.

items.title: Moved into a product.
items.body: Kit's quick fix: move the three to the nearest gaps — V3 to 545.0. But V1 is at 541.0 and V2 at 543.0, and 2 × 543.0 − 541.0 = 545.0. The ‘fixed’ V3 lands exactly on a third-order product of two mics nobody touched.
items.label: Test: where did the product land — and what's the lesson?
**Fix it:** re-coordinate the Playhouse around the new transmitter.

items.prompt: 11:45. How do you fix the plan?
items.happening: Three carriers must move without making new hits.
known: ◉ V3, V4, V5 in the channel
items.risk: A plan that fixes one conflict and makes another.
timeout: Kit's quick moves go to the contractor.

hints.text: After any move, what has to be rechecked?

options.label: Recompute the whole plan — every product against every carrier, with a guard off the new channel — and ask the venue coordinator for an on-site scan
options.result: V3 544.325, V4 555.325, V5 555.95 MHz: clean on paper, and clean on the coordinator's scan.
options.consequence: The plan as a system, proved where it's used.

options.label: Keep Kit's three quick moves
options.result: V3 hisses whenever V1 and V2 are both live — every duet.

options.label: Let the RF sub pick frequencies on the day
options.result: They pick them with a scanner at 6 p.m. on opening night.

items.title: The Radio Act of 1912
items.body: After the Titanic sank in April 1912, investigators found wireless traffic had been crowded and uncoordinated: operators talked over each other, and some ships didn't keep a radio watch. That August, the United States passed the Radio Act of 1912, requiring licences and assigning frequencies. Coordination has been part of radio ever since.

items.alt: The revised RFI answer: ‘YES. V3, V4, V5 re-coordinated; all products rechecked; coordinator scan attached. Checked: KB · MR.’
items.caption: An answer with its arithmetic — and two sets of initials.

items.title: On air since last month
items.body: The regulator's public database lists the new transmitter: licensed in March, on air last month. The RF plan was drawn in January. Spectrum changes; plans have dates.

items.prompt: Friday. How does the studio answer RFIs from now on?
timeout: The next quick answer goes out unchecked.

hints.text: What was missing on RFI 31 that the other 39 had?

options.label: Every RFI answer gets its check or calculation attached and a second person's initials, and RF plans are re-checked whenever the spectrum changes
options.result: Kit writes the RFI template himself — with a ‘checked by’ box.

options.label: Only Anselm answers RFIs
options.result: RFIs queue for a week; site stops.

options.label: Nothing — RFI 31 is fixed
options.result: RFI 44 is answered in five minutes next month.

items.alt: Kit showing Maya his new RFI template on screen, with a ‘checked by’ box.

bubbles.text: I put a box on it. For the next person who's ten minutes from a meeting.

items.title: Answered in 10 minutes
items.body: The studio's RFI log shows forty answers this year. Thirty-nine have a checker's initials. RFI 31 has none — the one answered ten minutes before the Playhouse meeting.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Third-order products: 2f₁ − f₂ and 2f₂ − f₁. After any move, recompute every product against every carrier, keep a guard off occupied spectrum, and have the venue’s coordinator scan it. Answer RFIs like designs: with the arithmetic and a second checker.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Kit was ten minutes from a meeting. What’s the quick answer you give when you’re rushed — and who checks it?
